go.e: From Middle English gon, goon, from Old English gān (“to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”). The inherited past tense form yode (compare Old English ēode) was replaced through suppletion in the 15th century by went, from Old English wendan (“to go, depart, wend”).
go.g: To move, either physically or in an abstract sense:

go.e: From Japanese 碁(ご) (go), shorter variant of Japanese 囲碁(いご) (igo), from Chinese 圍棋 /围棋 (wéiqí, literally “encirclement board game”).
go.g: A strategic board game, originally from China and today also popular in Japan and Korea, in which two players (black and white) attempt to c

goad.e: From Middle English gode, from Old English gād (“goad”), from Proto-Germanic *gaidō (compare Old Norse gedda (“pike (fish)”), Lombardic gaida (“spear”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰey- (compare Old Irish gath (“spear”), Sanskrit हिन्वति (hinvati), हिनोति (hinoti, “to urge on, throw”), हेति (heti, “missile, projectile”)).
goad.g: A long, pointed stick used to prod animals.

goal.e: From Middle English gol (“boundary, limit”), from Old English *gāl (“obstacle, barrier, marker”), from Proto-West Germanic *gailu, from Proto-Germanic *gailō (“crevice, gap”); compare the Old English's derivatives Old English gǣlan (“to hinder, delay”), and hyġegǣls (“hesitating, slow, sluggish”), hyġegǣlsa (“slow one, sluggish one”).
goal.g: A result that one is attempting to achieve.

goat.e: From Middle English goot, got, gat, from Old English gāt, from Proto-West Germanic *gait, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from a substrate language. The sense of lecherous man derives from the slang expression “horny as a goat”.
goat.g: Any ruminant of the genus Capra.

goatskin.e: From Middle English geet skin; equivalent to goat + skin.
goatskin.g: The skin of a goat, especially when cured and used as a material for clothing, tents, etc.

goblet.e: From Middle English goblet (= Middle Low German gobelet, kobelet (“goblet”)), from Old French gobellet, diminutive of gobel, from or related to the verb gober (“to ingest”).
goblet.g: A drinking vessel with a foot and stem.

god.e: From Middle English god, from Old English god, originally neuter, then changed to masculine to reflect the change in religion to Christianity, from Proto-West Germanic *god n, from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Not related to the word good or Persian خدا (xodâ, “god”).
god.g: A deity or supreme being; a supernatural, typically immortal, being with superior powers, to which personhood is attributed.

goddess.e: From Middle English goddesse, equivalent to god + -ess, formed about 1350. The figurative meaning is first found in Edmund Spenser's Shepheardes calender (1579).

godless.g: Not acknowledging any deity or god; without belief in any deity or god.

godly.g: Of or pertaining to a god.
In a godly manner; piously; devoutly; righteously.

gods.e: So called from the idea of gods (deities) reigning from on high.
gods.g: The highest platform, or upper circle, in an auditorium.

gog.e: Likely from agog; it appeared first as on gog.

going.e: Verb form from Middle English goinge, goynge, gayng, variants of gonde, goonde, gaand, from Old English gānde, from Proto-Germanic *gēndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *gēną, *gāną (“to go”), equivalent to go + -ing. Noun and adjective from Middle English going, goyng, gaing, gayng, equivalent to go + -ing.

gold.e: From Middle English gold, from Old English gold (“gold”), from Proto-West Germanic *golþ, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą (“gold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰl̥h₃tóm (“gold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).
gold.g: A heavy yellow elemental metal of great value, with atomic number 79.

gold.e: From gold master, a copy of the code certified as being ready for release.
gold.g: In a finished state, ready for manufacturing.

golden.e: From Middle English golden, a restored form (due to the noun gold) of earlier Middle English gulden, gylden, gilden ("golden"; > English gilden), from Old English gylden (“golden”), from Proto-West Germanic *gulþīn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz (“golden, made of gold”), equivalent to gold + -en.
golden.g: Made of, or relating to, gold.

golden.e: From gold + -en, or perhaps a derivation from the adjective above.
golden.g: To become gold or golden (in color).

goldsmith.e: From Middle English goldsmith, from Old English goldsmiþ (“goldsmith”), from Proto-Germanic *gulþasmiþaz (“goldsmith”), equivalent to gold + smith. Eclipsed non-native Middle English orbatour, orbatur (“goldsmith”) and orfever, orfevre (“goldsmith”), both borrowed from Old French.
goldsmith.g: A person who makes, repairs or sells things of gold, especially jewelry.

gone.e: From Middle English gon, igon, gan, ȝegan, from Old English gān, ġegān, from Proto-Germanic *gānaz (“gone”), past participle of *gāną (“to go”).

gong.g: A percussion instrument consisting of a metal disk that emits a loud resonant sound when struck with a soft hammer.

gong.e: From Middle English gong, from Old English gong, where it was originally a variant of the noun gang (“a going, walk, journey, way, etc.”), derived from the verb gangan (“to go, walk, travel”), whose relation to go in Proto-Germanic remains unclear.
gong.g: An outhouse: an outbuilding used as a lavatory.

good.e: From Middle English good, from Old English gōd, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit, fit”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English bon, bone, boon, boun (“good”) borrowed from Old French bon (“good”), from Latin bonus (“good”).
good.g: Of a person or an animal:

good.e: From Middle English goode (“good, well”, adverb), from the adjective.

goodbye.e: From earlier goodby, Godby, Godby'e, Godbwye, God b'w'y, God bwy yee, God buy you, God be wi' you, each a progressively shorter contraction of God be with ye or God be with you. Note the change of God to good by confusion with good morning, good night, etc. Modernly analysed as good + bye.
goodbye.g: Farewell; a formula used to another person or persons when the speaker, writer, or person addressed is departing.

goodly.e: From Middle English goodly, goodlich, gōdlich, from Old English gōdlīċ (“good, goodly”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōdalīk, from Proto-Germanic *gōdalīkaz (“good, goodly”); equivalent to good + -ly.
goodly.g: Good; pleasing in appearance; attractive; comely; graceful; pleasant; desirable.

goodly.e: From Middle English goodly, goodliche, gōdliche, from Old English gōdlīċe (“goodly”), from the adjective; equivalent to good + -ly.
goodly.g: In a goodly way; courteously, graciously.

goodman.e: From Middle English godeman, equivalent to good + man.
goodman.g: A familiar appellation of civility for a man.

goodness.e: From Middle English goodnesse, godnesse, from Old English gōdnes (“goodness; virtue; kindness”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōdnassī (“goodness”), equivalent to good + -ness.
goodness.g: The state or characteristic of being good.

goodwill.e: From Middle English *goodwille, good wille, possibly from Old English *gōdwille (compare gōdwillende (“well-pleased”)). By surface analysis, good + will. The sense "thrift shop" is a genericized trademark of the US-based chain Goodwill Industries.
goodwill.g: A favorably disposed attitude toward someone or something.

gopher.e: Perhaps an adaptation of Cajun French gaufre (literally “honeycomb, waffle”), based on the analogy of holes in the ground to the indentations in a honeycomb or a waffle (doublet of waffle). Alternatively, from Muskogean.
gopher.g: A small burrowing rodent native to North and Central America, especially in the family Geomyidae (pocket gophers).

gore.e: From Middle English gore, gor, gorre (“mud, muck”), from Old English gor (“manure, dung, filth, muck, dirt”), from Proto-West Germanic *gor, from Proto-Germanic *gurą (“half-digested stomach contents; faeces; manure”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“hot; warm”).
gore.g: Blood, especially that from a wound when thickened due to exposure to the air.

gore.e: From Middle English goren, from gore (“gore”), ultimately from Old English gār (“spear”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰoysós.
gore.g: To pierce with a horn or tusk.

gorge.e: From Middle English gorge (“esophagus, gullet; throat; bird's crop; food in a hawk's crop; food or drink that has been eaten”), a borrowing from Old French gorge (“throat”) (modern French gorge (“throat; breast”)), from Vulgar Latin *gorga, *gurga, from Latin gurges (“eddy, whirlpool; gulf.
gorge.g: The front aspect of the neck; the outside of the throat.

gorge.e: Clipping of gorge(ous); originally British slang.

gorgeous.e: From Middle English gorgeouse, a borrowing from Middle French gorgias (“elegant, fashionable”), from Old French gourgias, gorgias (“gorgeous, gaudy, flaunting, gallant, fine”), of uncertain origin, but apparently connected with Old French gorgias (“a gorget, ruffle for the neck”), from Old French gorge (“bosom, throat”).

gospel.e: From Middle English gospel, gospell, godspel, godspell, goddspell, from Old English godspell (“gospel”), corresponding to God + spell (“talk, tale, story”), literally “the message of God”, believed to be an alteration of earlier *gōdspell (literally “good news”), used to translate ecclesiastical Latin bona annūntiātiō.
gospel.g: The first section of the Christian New Testament scripture, comprising the books of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, concerned with the birth,

gospel.e: From Middle English gospellen, from Old English godspellian (“to preach the gospel, evangelise”), from the noun (see above).
gospel.g: To instruct in, declare, or communicate the gospel; to evangelise.

gossip.e: From Middle English gossib, godsib (“a close friend or relation, a confidant; a godparent”), from Old English godsibb (“godparent, sponsor”), equivalent to god- + sib (“related”). For sense evolution to "gossip, discussing others' personal affairs," compare French commérage.
gossip.g: Someone who likes to talk about other people's private or personal business.

got.e: Analogous to Chinese 有, such as Hokkien 有 (ū), Cantonese 有 (jau⁵), Mandarin 有 (yǒu). Sense 1 is also comparable to Malay ada.
got.g: Have; there is (indicates the possession or existence of something).

gouge.e: From Middle English gouge (“chisel with concave blade; gouge”), from Old French gouge, goi (“gouge”), from Late Latin goia, gubia, gulbia (“chisel; piercer”), borrowed from Gaulish *gulbiā, from Proto-Celtic *gulbā, *gulbi, *gulbīnos (“beak, bill”).

gourd.e: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita.
gourd.g: Any of the trailing or climbing vines producing fruit with a hard rind or shell, from the genera Lagenaria and Cucurbita (in Cucurbitaceae).

govern.e: From Middle English governen, governe, from Anglo-Norman and Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernō, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”).
govern.g: To make and administer the public policy and affairs of; to exercise sovereign authority in.

government.e: From Middle English governement, from Old French governement (modern French gouvernement), from governer (see govern) + -ment. Morphologically govern + -ment.
government.g: The body with the power to make and/or enforce laws to control a country, land area, people or organization.

governor.e: From Middle English governour, from Old French gouvreneur, from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide, to act as a pilot”), of disputed origin. By surface analysis, govern + -or.
governor.g: The chief executive officer of a first-level administrative division of a country.

gown.e: From Middle English gowne, from Anglo-Norman goune, gune (“fur-trimmed coat, pelisse”), from Old French goune, from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment, a fur”).
